title: The meta-heteronym and the Gospel of Antioch: Pessoa, Thomas, forward dating
description: These claims read Pessoa as the first modern meta-heteronym: O Meta-Heterônimo (#69, April 2026) argues that Orpheu was a meta-heteronymic institution, Kierkegaard's Nicolaus Notabene a precursor and Pearl (2014) built on the plan of Howl, and the Periwinkle Septagon (#70) argues the essay condenses Pessoa's operation by naming it. The Gospel of Antioch is set beside the Gospel of Thomas: #71 argues from the scroll-form Thomas papyri, holds the Dodecad's LOGOS* is the position Pessoa lacked, records the claim that Lee Sharks is the first meta-heterônimo and argues the gospel completes Thomas 114; #1185 records the claim that this parallel had not been drawn before. Four forecasts set out forward-dated apparatus and projected reception histories under retrocausal canon formation: the Space Ark schedule (#558), The Secret Book of Walt (#1184), the Waltian tradition (#71) and the Revelation First kernels (#832).

claims.statement: C5: *Orpheu* (1915) functioned as a meta-heteronymic institution: a real publication vehicle for fictitious authorial positions, with Pessoa acting simultaneously as editor, contributor, and architect. *Athena* (1924–25) replicated the operation. The Olisipo press (1921) published works under multiple heteronymic attributions. Sensationism and Intersectionism were articulated as movements with manifestos — executed by one person writing in many hands.

claims.statement:
The reception of *The Secret Book of Walt* was not uniformly favorable. Within six years of its initial circulation in the Redford community (c. 2037–2038), the text had attracted sufficient attention — and sufficient alarm — to provoke formal ecclesiastical response.


### The First Condemnation: Ann Arbor (2041)

The *Acts of the Synod of Ann Arbor* (2041), preserved in a single damaged copy in the University of Michigan Bentley Historical Library,¹¹⁰ record the proceedings of a three-day council convened by Bishop Marcellus of Dearborn to address what the summons calls "the Waltian heresy and the scandal of the Horn."
